name: Parametrised Post-Newtonian Metric
description: The weak gravitational field of a slowly moving body with a number in front of every term, so that each metric theory of gravity is a set of numbers and each experiment in the solar system measures a combination of them. General relativity is the point $\beta = \gamma = 1$, where the metric is Schwarzschild's far from the horizon.
convention: The mass enters as the length $m = GM/c^2$, and we keep factors of $c$ explicit. We count $v/c$ as first order and $m/r$ as second, and write the metric and its inverse whole. The connection, the Riemann tensor, and the Ricci tensor keep terms in $m^2$ where a component carries two time indices and stop at the first power of $m$ elsewhere, as the Einstein tensor, the Weyl tensor, and the Ricci scalar do throughout, and the Kretschmann scalar is its leading term. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: How much of general relativity do the experiments compel? The question is Arthur Eddington's, from his textbook of 1923, where he puts "three questions in crescendo" to the experiments: whether they "verify", "suggest", or "compel the laws we adopt" [eddington1923]. He took the static, spherically symmetric field of a particle and expanded it in powers of $1/r$ with an unknown coefficient on every term, $ds^2 = -(1 + a_1/r + a_2/r^2 + \dots)^{-1}dr^2 - r^2d\theta^2 - r^2\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2 + (1 + b_1/r + b_2/r^2 + b_3/r^3 + \dots)dt^2$ [eddington1923]. The observations then fill the coefficients in one at a time: Newton's law of gravitation "shows that $b_1 = -2m$", the deflection of light "then shows that $a_1 = -2m$", and the perihelion of Mercury "then shows that $b_2 = 0$" [eddington1923]. The last two, he warned, "are not determined experimentally with any high accuracy" [eddington1923]. He had helped measure one of them: the eclipse of 29 May 1919 gave a deflection at the Sun's limb of $1.98 \pm 0.12$ seconds of arc at Sobral and $1.61 \pm 0.30$ at Príncipe, where Einstein's theory asks for $1.75$ and Newton's for $0.87$ [dyson1920].¶In isotropic coordinates and today's letters the same field carries two numbers, $\beta$ and $\gamma$: $ds^2 = -\left(1 - 2m/r + 2\beta m^2/r^2\right)c^2dt^2 + \left(1 + 2\gamma m/r\right)\left(dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2\right)$, with $m = GM/c^2$ and $r^2 = x^2 + y^2 + z^2$, which Kip Thorne and Clifford Will call "the original Eddington (1922)-Robertson (1962)-Schiff (1967) version of the PPN formalism" [thornewill1971]. The number $\gamma$ is "the amount of space-curvature which a standard mass produces", and $\beta$ measures "the extent of nonlinearity of post-Newtonian gravity", since in most theories "gravity itself also produces gravity" [willnordtvedt1972]. For Leonard Schiff, writing in 1960, the deflection of light followed from the equivalence principle and special relativity, so that "only the planetary orbit precession provides a real test of general relativity" [schiff1960tests]. Light grazing the Sun is bent by $\tfrac{1}{2}(1 + \gamma)$ times $1.7505$ seconds of arc: Einstein's calculation of 1911, from the equivalence principle alone, is the first half, which "holds in any metric theory", and the curvature of space around the Sun is the second, which "varies from theory to theory" [will2014]. Mercury's perihelion advances by $\tfrac{1}{3}(2 + 2\gamma - \beta)$ times $42.98$ seconds of arc a century, the Sun's oblateness left out [will2014]. General relativity is the point $\beta = \gamma = 1$, and Carl Brans and Robert Dicke's theory of 1961 lies at $\beta = 1$, $\gamma = (1 + \omega)/(2 + \omega)$, with $\omega$ its coupling constant [thornewill1971, bransdicke1961].¶Does the Earth fall toward the Sun exactly as the Moon does? Kenneth Nordtvedt saw that the measured equality of inertial and gravitational mass says nothing about the part of a body's mass that is its gravitational self energy, and that experiments with astronomical bodies could [nordtvedt1968a]. To see what the theories predict he "began over again", in Thorne and Will's words, with the post-Newtonian equations of motion for point masses, "adding several terms which are absent in general relativity but could be present in other theories, and by putting an arbitrary parameter in front of each term" [thornewill1971]. In Einstein's theory the two masses came out equal, and in Brans and Dicke's they differed "by a term of the order of the massive body's gravitational self-energy divided by its total energy" [nordtvedt1968b]. The Moon is where it would show: if the Earth's self energy falls differently, "the lunar orbit will acquire a range oscillation of amplitude about 12 m", within reach of laser ranging [nordtvedt1968c]. Irwin Shapiro's "Fourth Test" of 1964 had meanwhile joined the three classical ones: the delay of a radar echo whose path to a planet and back passes the Sun, which comes to $\tfrac{1}{2}(1 + \gamma)$ times about 250 microseconds for a signal that just grazes it [shapiro1964, will2014, reasenberg1979].¶By August 1970 Thorne and Will could list what two numbers left out: the dragging of inertial frames by the rotating Earth, which a gyroscope in orbit would feel, periodic terms in the distance from the Earth to the Moon, and Nordtvedt's breakdown of free fall for the Earth [thornewill1971]. They wrote as theorists who were "hamstrung: Experiment has not yet told us which relativistic theory of gravity is correct", and as realists about the bill: "(We can expect the megabuck to be a useful unit of measure for some of the tests.)" [thornewill1971]. Their framework "takes the slow-motion, post-Newtonian limit of all conceivable metric theories and characterizes that limit by a set of nine real-valued parameters", so that each theory is a point in a space of nine dimensions and each experiment a measurement of its coordinates [thornewill1971]. Will extended the framework to a perfect fluid, putting parameters into Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar's post-Newtonian hydrodynamics, and gave the "Nordtvedt effect" its name [will1971]. In 1972 he and Nordtvedt, who had each "originally used his own set of PPN parameters", joined their notations into nine that sort theories by how much a mass curves space, how nonlinear gravity is, whether the universe has a preferred frame of rest, and whether momentum is conserved [willnordtvedt1972]. The count now stands at ten [will2014].¶Radar echoes from Mercury and Venus gave Shapiro and his colleagues $\tfrac{1}{2}(1 + \gamma) = 1.02$ in 1971, with an uncertainty they put at $0.05$ to allow for systematic errors [shapiro1971]. Ranging to the Viking spacecraft at Mars for 14 months, through the superior conjunction of 25 November 1976, brought $\gamma = 1.000 \pm 0.002$ [reasenberg1979]. At Cassini's conjunction of 2002 the spacecraft was $8.43$ astronomical units from the Sun and its radio signals passed within $1.6$ solar radii of it, on two frequency bands that kept the effects of the solar corona down [will2014]. From the frequency shift of that link Bruno Bertotti, Luciano Iess, and Paolo Tortora found $\gamma = 1 + (2.1 \pm 2.3) \times 10^{-5}$ [bertotti2003]. Brans and Dicke's $\omega$ then has to exceed $40{,}000$ [will2014].¶Mercury's orbit, fitted with data from the Messenger spacecraft and with Cassini's $\gamma$ put in, gives $\beta - 1 = (-4.1 \pm 7.8) \times 10^{-5}$ [will2014]. The Moon has been ranged by laser since August 1969, off Apollo 11's reflector, and Nordtvedt's oscillation has not appeared: $4\beta - \gamma - 3 = (4.4 \pm 4.5) \times 10^{-4}$ [will2014, williams2004]. Schiff's gyroscope flew in 2004 as Gravity Probe B and found the dragging of frames by the Earth, which the parametrised metric sets at $\tfrac{1}{2}\left(1 + \gamma + \tfrac{1}{4}\alpha_1\right)$ times general relativity's rate, with $\alpha_1$ one of Will and Nordtvedt's preferred frame parameters, to 20 percent [schiff1960, will2014, everitt2011]. Today $\gamma$ is $1$ to within $2.3$ parts in $10^5$ and $\beta$ to within $8$ [will2014].

related.text: General relativity's point of the plane. At $\beta = \gamma = 1$ the metric is Schwarzschild's in isotropic coordinates, expanded far from the horizon [thornewill1971].

The slowly rotating star of general relativity. Far from it Hartle and Thorne's field is Lense and Thirring's, which is the rotating body here at $\beta = \gamma = 1$ and $\alpha_1 = 0$, to first order in the mass [will2014].
The body taken away. At $m = 0$ every number in front of every term has nothing left to multiply, and the metric is flat.
Nordström's scalar theory as a point of the plane. At $\gamma = -1$ and $\beta = 1/2$ the metric is the weak field of his point mass, which bends no light [deruelle2011].

A metric with no horizon that sits at general relativity's point: $e^{-2m/r} = 1 - 2m/r + 2m^2/r^2 - \dots$, so $\beta = \gamma = 1$ and the post-Newtonian tests do not separate the two [boonserm2018].

Einstein's static gravity of 1912 as a point of the plane. At $\gamma = 0$ space is flat and light bends by half of general relativity's angle, with $\beta = 1/2$ by his equation of February and $3/4$ by that of March [will2014].
Brans and Dicke's theory as a point of the plane. Far from the body their static sphere has $\beta = 1$ and $\gamma = (1 + \omega)/(2 + \omega)$ [thornewill1971, bransdicke1961].
General relativity's field of many moving bodies, to the same order. One body at rest there is this metric at $\beta = \gamma = 1$ [will2014].

coordinates.name: Eddington-Robertson-Schiff (isotropic)
domains: r = R \;\text{(the surface of the body)}

parameters.description: Mass of the body as a length, $m = GM/c^2$
Eddington's number in front of $m^2/r^2$ in $g_{tt}$, the nonlinearity in the superposition of gravity; general relativity has $\beta = 1$
Eddington's number in front of $m/r$ in the metric of space, the curvature of space a unit of mass produces; general relativity has $\gamma = 1$
Radius of the body's surface, with $R \gg m$; the body itself fills $r < R$

coordinates.convention: We use isotropic coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, and take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, so a dot on $t$ in the geodesic equations means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.convention: We use isotropic coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, count $a/r$ as first order, so that a component with one time index keeps its term in $am$, and take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, so a dot on $t$ in the geodesic equations means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
coordinates.line_element: ds^2 = -\left(1 - \dfrac{2m}{r} + \dfrac{2\beta m^2}{r^2}\right)c^2dt^2 + \left(1 + \dfrac{2\gamma m}{r}\right)\left(dr^2 + r^2d\theta^2 + r^2\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2\right) - \dfrac{4\Delta am\sin^2\theta}{r}c\,dt\,d\phi
